The textbook readings, the corresponding questions, and the reflection papers that follow did not help me in the course but distracted me from preparing for the speeches themselves. Having to plan and practice, and sometimes even deliver, a speech without knowing how I did on the last one made it difficult to grow and learn from mistakes. A small tweak that would help the course is changing the order of the speeches. The cultural foundations (third) speech would have been a good way of getting to know our classmates, so it could have been first. The impromptu (first) speech was a difficult one to start with, so it could have come later. Essentially, swapping the first and third speeches would have made the progression feel more natural. It's an 8AM class in a big lecture hall, and as people are desperately trying to scribble down notes from the slides going by at Mach speed, sometimes the professor will pause, look at us and say out of nowhere, 'Let's have a quiz.' And just like that, pop quiz. Every time. We have never had a single planned quiz or test, other than our midterm and final. My friends will say, 'Ugh, I can't miss this class tomorrow, we have a quiz I need to study for!' and I cannot relate, because never once has this professor said, 'By the way, we're going to have a quiz tomorrow/next week/on Monday.' Improvement Comments:
1. Surprise assignments at the worst possible time
This was the absolute worst part of the class for me. The professor assigned a surprise several-hour long assignment, due right over thanksgiving break along with a 50 page reading, and a 500-page book to read, plus a 3 page reading review. The assignment was not on the syllabus, so students had their study plans according what was originally on the syllabus. The worst part-- it was assigned right around finals. This several hour assignment delayed my study plans so bad that I was unable to catch up on my other classes, which I had planned for the break. I messed up my other finals so bad because of this surprise assignment that I got an A- and a B in a classes I could have gotten an As in. The best part of all this? She couldn't even be bothered to grade the assignment. 

2. Unrealistic expectations
There is too much work in this class. No 300-level class is this much work. I don't care about too much work but the amount of work this class gives is unrealistic and the class should be four credits if it is this much. 40-50 page readings every single week, 500-word responses, a 300 or 500 page book and book review due over a holiday, a 12-15 page research paper due right before a final, and a surprise several-hour long assignment added to all this just for fun. There is no possible way to manage your time to finish these assignments in a timely manner. You will not be able to start the paper or book early, because you are swamped with other work she assigns until the weekend it is due. No matter how great you are of a student, the work is literally, physically impossible to manage.

3. Late grading, or no grading at all
For how much work she assigns, the professor can't be bothered to grade anything on time. She grades things so late so that you don't know how you are doing in the class and must delay the work you are doing. For her optional 6 out of 10 reading responses, she graded some of us so late that even if we wanted to start them early to get them out of the way, we were unable to due to the fact that she did not even release our grades early enough for us to know how we were doing on them. We were essentially forced to start the reading responses late, unless we wanted to continue doing them, not knowing if we were doing them right or not. This leads to work accumulating so much by the end of the semester that it severely impacts performance not only in this class, but other classes as well. Moreover, she grades so abstractly that one cannot understand how she grades. Some students who study hard and try in the class seem to get lower grades. Some students who barely studied got higher grades. This makes me suspicious of bias. This ruins motivation because students start to feel that no matter how hard they try in the class or how good the quality of their work is, the grading is so inconsistent that none of their effort even matters.
Also, she assigned a several-hour surprise assignment, which pushed many students to spend their entire Thanksgiving breaks doing homework for this class. However, she never even bothered to grade this assignment. She expects us to do so much work but she doesn't even do her part of it.

4. No distractions- unless it's your phone. 
Her lecture slides combined with her actual lectures have way too much information on them, but students cannot use their laptops. She doesn't upload slides either. Eventually, students started to use their phones to take pictures of the slides, because it is physically impossible to write everything down in time. What is totally ironic about this is that for how much she is against students using laptops, her students must resort to their phones for lecture slides. So, even if we're can't use our laptops (despite needing them for academic purposes), we end up using our phones anyway, which are also a distraction, if not more so than a laptop.

Overall, this was an unreasonably stressful class. The work would have been fine if she stuck to the syllabus and did not give a surprise several hour assignment during finals. This messed up a lot of students in their final stretch. She could have let us know and we would have planned around it.

Valuable Comments: This is the first semester where Seo taught a class at SBU, and I can honestly say she's become one of my favorite CME professors. She made an otherwise very difficult class digestible, and she was engaging and enthusiastic throughout. This was one of the few CME classes I did not find myself zoning out from. I especially enjoyed the Think Pair Shares, where we got to practice a bunch of problems in small groups during class time. The exams and grading were also very straightforward. Just for reference: A = 85, MT1 and MT2 are 29% each, final is 40%, attendance is 2%, and portfolio is +2% extra credit. Attendance is taken 4x, and she always announces the date ahead of time. The exams are closed book, but numerous reference tables are provided. The exams have 85% 'class problems' (those reviewed on the slides with number changes/minor tweaks at most), and 15% 'challenge problems' (could be any format: harder class problems, experimental design, trivia, etc). I honestly liked not having homework for this class, because that VASTLY reduced the workload this semester...previously, Junior Spring was known as one of the most work-intensive for CME, but that was not the case for us. Honestly though, having a small number of HWs or additional (ungraded) practice problems would help with exam prep. Seo also genuinely cares about us and wants to see us succeed. Improvement Comments:
The course has a lot of room for improvement. 

The delivery of the course content needs a lot of fine-tuning. As a fully online course for a fully-online program (EEO),  I expected a more streamlined online experience. The delivery seemed adequate if this were an offline class forced to move online due to the pandemic. This class, however, is advertised as part of the Electrical Engineering Online curriculum, which is supposedly meant to be accessible and accomodating to students without the luxury of attending in-person due to work scheduling or other obligations. 

Because of this, and the fact that the online program is several years old, I expected that most class materials would already exist, and would ideally be released at the beginning of each week. Releasing at the beginning of the week allows students to begin studying and working on classwork as soon as they have free time, rather than waiting an unknown length of time for materials to be released. I've found this to be helpful in previous online classes I've taken at other colleges.

Although the lectures (Zoom meetings) are recorded, in most cases, there was no guarantee when they would be posted for viewing if a student was unable to attend the live meeting, or if they simply wanted to review the lecture. Sometimes, it was posted the next day and other times, it wouldn't be posted for several days. This means that an online, nontraditional learner who may not be free at the scheduled time, is already behind through no fault of their own. 

The lecture notes and sample problem sets often contained typos or other errors which make understanding the material very difficult. 

The approach to grading and feedback leaves much to be desired. Ideally, the grading would be consistent, and the expectations would be more clear. On homework, sometimes a small error would result in a small amount of credit being lost, but at other times, a similar error would result in a substantial loss of credit. Additionally, the feedback on the assignments was almost non-existent. Most of the time, the feedback was nothing more than the statement 'wrong.' This is not helpful in learning from mistakes. Although the solutions are posted eventually, it would be helpful to get a little more feedback on individual homework mistakes. A final note on grading is that it it often takes weeks for grades to be released. Perhaps having additional TAs would help in this regard. In my case, my final homework assignment is still awaiting grading, at the time of writing this (one month after the due date, and four days prior to the final exam).

As far as exams are considered, I believe it would be beneficial to have at least one or two more exams worth a smaller percentage of the grade. Currently, the midterm and final exam make up 40% of the class grade each. Considering the amount of information that could be on each exam, it seems unfair that a single exam grade is weighted so high. Perhaps, this would be more acceptable if students were given more clear guidance on what would be covered on each exam rather than 'Everything from the beginning of the semester.'  Having a more specific idea of what is important with regard to the exams would allow a student to better focus their studies on a few particular areas rather than spending hours on subjects that are potentially of little importance.

I've found that the suggested textbook is of little help for this class. The approach to the subject seems to be unique, a fact Professor Parekh seems to take pride in. This may be fine for some students, but for those that need a little bit of extra help or clarification, this adds an extra layer of difficulty. The textbook does not provide a lot of insight into the topics as they are covered in this class, nor do online resources. This means that although there is plenty of information available both online and in the textbook, very little of it can be applied to this class if a student needs additional help on a particular subject. Additionally, there is, in my opinion, too much focus on the mathematical theory of electromagnetics and too little focus on applications. The textbook Fundamentals of Applied Electromagnetics, on the other hand, seems to strike a better balance, but again, is ultimately of little help in this class.

Finally, for a little background: this class is my first class at Stony Brook. I have an Associate's degree in Electronics, and due to my location and work committments, I am unable to enroll at an in-person engineering school. I was initially excited to learn of Stony Brook's Electrical Engineering Online program as it was advertised as the exact type of program for my needs (flexible scheduling, etc). Additionally, the fact that this was an entirely internet-based program led me to believe the courses would be optimized for internet-based learning. Unfortunately, this has not been my experience, and I am more than a little disappointed. I hope some of the issues I've mentioned will be corrected for future students.

Firstly, he repeats himself during each lecture and from one lecture to another often going over points that have been previously discussed. Many lectures start with a ‘quick recap’ often turning into lengthy reviews of previously covered material, leaving little time for new content. Most of the class time ends up being just lecturing, which makes it more of an analysis class, then a practical music theory class. Furthermore, he is very specific about subjects which are not related to the class. He spent too much time at the piano. For instance, it is unnecessary and offensive to show music majors that different registers of the same note exist. Student engagement is kept to its absolute minimum, and most of the time, student’s points are not properly acknowledged. He often outright calls student answers incorrect, while later in the lecture makes the same point. It feels disheartening, and discourages participation. The professor makes it very clear that he thinks highly of himself with all of the lecturing and dismissals, above what the students are. He obviously knows more, but brings students down. Additionally, Dr. Sheehy assigns very vague homework assignments. The directions and tasks are often confusing and leave students wondering if their work is meeting the professor’s standards. He also takes a very long time to grade homework. The lack of feedback makes it even harder to understand the assignments and grading standards. On the topic of being late, besides the first class, there was not a single time in the semester where we were not behind on the syllabus. Always “rushing to get back on track,” yet always falling even further behind. The class fostered no relationships between students and felt very isolated. Hearing each other's pieces could have been beneficial, helping students build relationships and better understand the vague assignments. Most importantly to me, the professor is unable to make changes to the class structure, despite students asking for help in the classroom due to their ongoing confusion and frustration. This class fell more than flat, it made me miserable and frustrated. I dreaded coming to every class. While I know this particular class is not going to exist after the curriculum change, I am of the firm opinion that Dr. Sheehy is not a good professor by any means and has a lot to learn as an educator. | There are innumerable ways this course could have been improved. Valuable Comments: The instructor Professor Zeng is a very valuable teacher within the Stony Brook community as a whole. I'm graduating this semester, and in my 4 years here, I haven't met any other instructor that is as dedicated to wanting students to learn. It is obvious that she really cares and is super passionate about teaching and most likely dedicates a lot of time outside of the classroom to lifelong learning. Also, she really takes students' feedback into account, which is more than I can say for a lot of professors I've had previously.     As one of the only non-native-Chinese speakers in the class, I was constantly on the edge of my seat as I wouldn't fully understand what was being said in class at any given moment, either because of grammar or because of vocabulary. That being said, I think it's valuable that most of what is spoken in class (unless necessary) is said in Chinese, and not English. This way, I was able to get fully immersed in the language, which wouldn't happen elsewhere, and which also didn't happen in the first part to this course (which was a lot easier).     Coming from one of the few non-native speakers in the class (I think there was 3 of us), I would say that Professor Zeng is very attentive to us specifically, and tries her best to ensure that we don't fall behind. It is a very fast paced course, but given the amount of time that you have to put into class doing homework assignments, studying for quizzes, attending mandatory office hours with TAs where you get to speak with them, and studying for tests, the way the course is set up pretty much ensures that you are constantly studying and therefore you won't fall through the cracks. Just know that if you do take this course, the professor really values feedback, and will take it into account. I really enjoyed the course, and would highly recommend it to anyone that wants to learn Chinese.    Also, the course content was structured in a way that made sense. I liked how the chapters covered topics that are relevant to our daily lives like visiting a doctor or making a phone call. | I love how the course attempts to teach you day to day Chinese, even if it differs from the textbook a bit. It's a bit rigorous at times because of pacing, but I feel like just going to class and doing all of the work required of you gets you to a good understanding of Chinese alone. Personally, I liked how while we were learning Chinese as a language, we also had discussions comparing our cultures to Chinese culture. It was nice to learn about my heritage as well as my classmates. The professor is also very nice and understanding, and you can always talk to her or the TAs if you're struggling and they genuinely try to help. It's really nice that she's constantly asking for feedback in TA Time, so even if people don't really speak up about it in class or directly go to her, they can still have some way to talk about it from doing work. | The amount of class and homework we have is significant to actually learning the language because it helps us practice. Professor DongMei genuinely wants all her students to be able to think critically and understand the Mandarin language. The activities she assigns help to reinforce the vocabulary and grammar we learn. 10/10 would recommend this class. | I think the most valuable part of this course was our biweekly reflections that we wrote and the teacher reading it to take into account for future lessons. I believe this really helped since it allowed us to be honest about what we were struggling on in the course and the professor reading it to spend more time on those lessons. | How supportive the professor and TAs are. They encourage us to speak in chinese, which betters our communicative abilities for the language. It helped build my confidence in speaking chinese with my peers.
Improvement Comments: That being said, there is a LOT of homework, which makes sense for a 4 credit course. I probably spent on average about 1 hour memorizing 12-13 new vocab before each quiz, and quizzes occur 1-2 times a week. Also, after trying to memorize the vocab, I would have to study the grammar to accompany the vocab. That being said, I only spent this much time studying because I took this course out of interest, actually want to learn the language, and want an A in this course. So, theoretically, you don't have to spend that much time studying, especially if you already have some background knowledge of the language (like if your parents speak it at home). But if you are a non-native-Chinese speaker, you will have to put in (likely) about 1.5x the amount of effort as those who are native speakers. So, if you don't have time to spare, if you're taking a large courseload or have difficult classes and don't think you'll have time, just know that this would definitely add to time spent studying outside of the classroom.     Also, I wish there was a bit more emphasis on learning random words simultaneously that are used in regular conversations (e.g. 'I don't agree' or 'actually'), because those aren't really taught in the book. That being said, that would add to the already heavy course, and I don't think there is enough time to incorporate that into the course. | I think it's already good as it is, as I haven't had any issues other than how rigorous it feels like the pacing picked up compared to CHI 111, but I know that can't really be helped due to the curriculum and the time we have. There are a number of ways that this course could be improved.

First and most important, the TA's for the recitation classes should be proficient enough in English to teach material. Professor McDonnell is a good teacher and is obviously passionate about his work but the recitation courses for this class were difficult to go to, and I eventually stopped going since I felt like it was a waste of my time since communication was so difficult.

Valuable Comments: I'm writing this response more for students than the professor as I put my constructive feedback in the 'In what ways, if any, could the course be improved' section. This course requires a lot of time and effort, and your grade may or may not reflect this depending on how good you are at test taking. The points in the course are primarily from exams, but both exams and homework are graded very harshly where if any ambiguity exists it will be counted against you. The first midterm is the easiest, the second midterm is the hardest, and the final is typically between the difficulty of the midterms according to the professor and class averages. Thus, it is very important to study by practicing large topics and reviewing the smaller ones as something briefly talked about in class could be 1/8 of the test. Also, the practice exam may not be good indicators of what will be on the exams as it can vary. The class uses questions from the textbook for the homework, but the homework is submitted as PDFs instead of through the textbook. Assignments can be quite tedious as they might have up to ~50ish problems for the long ones. Overall, this class will take up much of your time for doing homework and studying, and its grading is harsh. Likely, you'll have to take this course for the major requirement; however, if you want to learn discrete mathematics, I'd recommend learning it from the textbook on Dr. Ganapathi's website instead of from this class as most of the lecture's content comes from it, and you won't become burdened from the excessive workload of this class. | It instilled within me the kind of primal fear that mankind felt in the days of caves and foragers, when lightning would strike the ground in front of them and destroy the dirt beneath it, as if a god had seen fit to punish it. | Probably the homework assignments are the most valuable in memorizing and applying the material. Assignments are quite long and tedious, and while I do understand the need for practice, the length encourages students to rush through them instead of taking time to fully grasp the problem. My biggest complaint with the class is the professor stresses the importance of the structure or form of the reasoning stating, 'We care for reasoning not correctness'; however, there aren't any good examples showcasing the form for proofs. Many proofs are missing one or more components of the proof that are required on the exams such as conclusions, all the reasoning, or explicit p statements, and these discrepancies mislead students to think they aren't required as they are neglected in the slide examples. I understand when the professor skips these parts for the sake of time during demonstrations; however, he should make it more explicitly clear what is required and how proofs will be graded. Something that would greatly increase understanding is if the professor gave a guide to students on how proofs are graded and how many points are deducted for what mistakes; the assignments in the class are typically graded so close to the exams or after the exams that they can't be used to understand what mistakes one should fix, and the exams are graded so harshly that these problems cost people many points. Valuable Comments:

This could be improved by assigning specific readings to each lecture. Almost every quiz and assignment was postponed from the dates proposed in the syllabus and the final quiz was cancelled due to one photocopier machine being out order, despite the fact that there are plenty of printer and photocopying devices around campus. Several student were depending on that quiz to help their grade, and it was unnecessarily cancelled. There was very little guidance in helping students prepare for the papers and the quizzes, it was very hard to expect what would be on the quiz. Improvement Comments:
As much as I *loved* this class, I do think there were some major flaws.  First, the syllabus was confusing and seemed incomplete. For example, the required readings were not made clear until students asked about it after the first class. Also, according to the syllabus, there were supposed to be open office hours, but I tried to attend twice and both times the Zoom meeting was not active.  Second, there was a lot of repetition when we were learning from the slideshows. In the first half of the semester, we would often spend the first 10-20 minutes of class going over the exact same slides that we had seen at the end of the previous class. We sometimes also re-watched videos partially or fully. Even when we weren't using slides, the professor would often repeat things verbatim from earlier in the class or previous classes. I understand how repetition helps drive a point home, but this was excessive.  Finally, I think we watched too many videos in class. All of the videos were great, but most of them could have been assigned as homework. I'm not usually in favor of getting more homework, but we had entire classes where we watched as many as 3 lengthy back to back videos. I don't want to spend my tuition on videos that I can watch on YouTube for free in my own time. We weren't able to cover all of the main language families of the world, but we would have had more time to do so if the videos were assigned for outside of class time. | I do not want to offend Professor Ordonez and say anything inappropriate, but in my opinion he has a thick accent which makes it hard for students to understand.

And Dr. Burgueno was successful in satisfying the large intellectual curiosity many of us had about structures.    I also appreciated his coverage of vibrations which surprisingly had content that was not even covered in CIV 432, like how lumped masses are actually found and how the stiffness matrix can be obtained in an easier fashion. | Dr. Burgueno's passion for the material, his ability to teach the material efficiently, and the ability to now understand structural systems, software, etc. to a much higher level of confidence. Improvement Comments: The Direct Stiffness Section of the course felt a bit rushed. I understand that Dr. Burgueno wanted to reach vibrations and nonlinear analysis in the end so time had to be sacrificed. While the packets he made for Direct Stiffness were very helpful, I believe there were not enough practice problems covered. In particular, dealing with the structural load vector. We had one example with only span loads and another example with only nodal loads; but we never had an example with both types of loads at the same time. Essentially, he never covered how the structural load vector was supposed to be compiled in the general case.     This critique may seem very specific and insignificant if it were not for the fact that 80% of the final was on Direct Stiffness Method. Additionally, he kept saying that in the final, we would get to chose whichever method to solve the structure; and he emphasized that we needed to review all the methods to see which one would be better. I believe Dr. Burgueno failed in showing the importance of other methods based on the final that he gave. And it really confirms to me that the flexibility method is the most useless method in all of structural engineering.

Improvement Comments: As someone who has taken Programming courses for over 5 years in high school and college (3 of which were college courses or college equivalent courses in high school), I firmly believe that tests that require hand-writing code are useless, and are extremely inaccurate tests of programming ability and understanding. A core component of the programming process is debugging and trying different methods to see what can work and what can't. The ability to write programs from memory uses totally different skills than writing programs in an IDE. And the ability to do so is in the end, useless. If the exams were done in the way that the online homework was, for example, the programs on the exams would be able to be much more complicated, and would much better reflect a persons ability to program the concepts covered in the class. Instead, the programs on the exams ask for students to create extraordinarily simple programs, and the only part of the process that is hard is the hand writing of the code, instead of the hard part being coming up with algorithms and methods to solve complex problems. It's the difference between 'Can you memorize and regurgitate what we went over in class' vs. 'Can you take what we learned in class and apply it to new problems'. There are many ways to do programming course exams that do not include hand-written code, and every one of them is a better way to test programming ability. | I think the pace is too fast. The course itself felt very disorganized, and Professor Tripathi did not really have control of this because the course was directed by Professor Tashbook. I wish Professor Tripathi did have more control over the course because it felt like Professor Tashbook was taking on too much work alone. Throughout the semester, the students waited for Homeworks 3, 4, and 5 to be released. We were given Homework 3 and the final project during Thanksgiving break and were given ~2 weeks to complete them (which got extended to 3 weeks eventually). We were also promised extra credit to be assigned with Homework 3 and the final project, but Professor Tashbook did not assign the extra credit until the morning of the due date. He did not provide extra credit for Homework 3, but he did for the final project and gave us an additional 2 day extension for the final project. I also wish the tests were less verbose. The final exam was well-written, but the two midterms were so verbose, and I felt I spent more time reading and trying to understand the prompts than actually answering the problems. I'd rather the labs or homeworks be more verbose as we would have more time to spend per problem.

My biggest problem, however, is not so much the disorganization of the course as is the attitude Professor Tashbook gave off towards the end of the semester. In one instance, he emailed the students a long email saying he's being pulled in 27 different directions and doesn't have time to do anything. He then continued by saying that his TAs that were trying to be 'helpful' (with the quotation marks included in the email) were counterproductive. He called them self-appointed lawyers for trying to teach concepts that they thought were necessary to succeed in not just the class, but the entire major. Basically, the entire paragraph he had about them gave the tone that he was ungrateful for his TAs. There is clearly a lack of communication between the professor and the TAs, and this would not have been a problem had the professor been clear from the very beginning about his agenda for the semester. It is therefore unfair to be pushing the blame on the TAs that were only trying to help despite being given no information.

Great lecturer. Labs get hard and HWs are even harder. Need to apply more than what you learn in class to do the HW. HWs are harder tasks than the things you do in class. There are a lot of in class examples that also implement ideas from other studies, like math, biology, or sports. Attendance in lab (except some) is not required and 20/25 of them count towards your grade. You have TAs there to help, and if you don't complete it on time but are sitting in the room, you get full credit for the lab session. There is extra coding practice and a piazza if you need help. 2 Midterms and one final. Final is cumulative. Don't need to code at all on any. However, the second midterm still has topics from the first units. He will say that he needs to put the beginnings because the units build off each other, but you should still study the beginning units again. Also study the past exam(s), which he gives back to you and also returns your answers and what you got wrong. This is very helpful. He also gives you extra practice on the Exams/Quizzes section, but the 'not' practice exams he gives you and tells you that 'they are not practice, they are just the exams he gave last semester' has questions that are more similar (and easier) to what your midterm will be like than the ones that are on the Exams/Quizzes section. Improvement Comments: This BIO 310 Cell Biology course was, without exaggeration, the most poorly designed and mismanaged undergraduate course I’ve encountered. The professors—an adjunct lecturer with a PhD from Bulgaria (1992) and an instructional support technician with an MA —were not credible instructors for a course of this magnitude. Neither created original lecture content; instead, they relied entirely on borrowed materials from colleagues, including pre-recorded videos and slide decks. There was no actual instruction, no guidance, and no meaningful engagement throughout this asynchronous 8-week course.    The workload was excessive and pedagogically unjustified: 3 exams, 9 quizzes, 4 peer reviews, 2 self-assessments, 2 video presentations, and an academic integrity quiz. Yet exams alone accounted for 75% of the final grade. Each exam covered over 500 slides spanning 9 lectures, and included topics far beyond the scope of cell biology—epidemiology and public health, microbiology, genetics, cancer biology, immunology, developmental biology, and more. This was not a cell biology course; it was a disorganized survey of graduate-level biomedical science.    To make matters worse, the professors made two clear errors on the second exam and refused to throw out the faulty questions. Instead, they arbitrarily awarded two bonus points—despite the flawed questions totaling eight points. A fair adjustment would have been to either award six more points or reduce the denominator from 25 to 23. Their refusal to correct this undermines academic integrity.    There was no way to track grades until the final two weeks, no access to a class roster, and no meaningful support via email. I hired a professional tutor—a PhD cell biologist with postdoctoral experience—who confirmed this course was graduate-level in both depth and workload. He advised me to drop it, calling it “insane, biased, and unfair.”    Despite studying eight hours daily for 2.5 weeks per exam, I averaged only 70%. I’ve taken multiple 400-level biology courses at SUNY Plattsburgh, including BIO 401, and none approached the difficulty or dysfunction of BIO 310. This course was a pedagogical failure and should be completely restructured or removed from the undergraduate curriculum. | I found the lack of office hours difficult if extra help was needed, more office hours and professor availability would be an improvement; materials to prep for tests or lectures were not always made available in a timely fashion - it would have been helpful to have everything posted at the beginning of the course; 75% of the grade being based on 3 multiple choice tests I don't feel best reflects my effort and grasp of the concepts in the class - I would recommend in the future allowing students to explain answers for partial credit or having more homework assignments to demonstrate effort and understanding. | I think that the test questions could greatly be improved.
